{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
{{onesource|date=November 2009}}
In mathematics, the '''secondary measure''' associated with a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] of positive [[density]] ρ when there is one, is a measure of positive density μ, turning the [[secondary polynomials]] associated with the [[orthogonal polynomials]] for ρ into an orthogonal system.

==Introduction==
Under certain assumptions, it is possible to obtain the existence of  a secondary measure and even to express it. 

For example, this can be done when working in the [[Hilbert space]] ''L''<sup>2</sup>([0, 1], '''R''', ρ)

: <math> \forall x \in [0,1], \qquad \mu(x)=\frac{\rho(x)}{\frac{\varphi^2(x)}{4} + \pi^2\rho^2(x)}</math>

with

: <math> \varphi(x) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} 2\int_0^1\frac{(x-t)\rho(t)}{(x-t)^2+\varepsilon^2} \, dt </math>

in the general case, or:

: <math> \varphi(x) = 2\rho(x)\text{ln}\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right) - 2 \int_0^1\frac{\rho(t)-\rho(x)}{t-x} \, dt</math>

when ρ satisfies a [[Lipschitz condition]].

This application φ is called the reducer of ρ.

More generally, μ et ρ are linked by their [[Stieltjes transformation]] with the following formula:

: <math>S_{\mu}(z)=z-c_1-\frac{1}{S_{\rho}(z)}</math>

in which ''c''<sub>1</sub> is the [[moment (mathematics)|moment]] of order 1 of the measure ρ.

Secondary measures and the theory around them may be used to derive traditional formulas of analysis concerning the [[Gamma function]],  the [[Riemann zeta function]], and the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].

They have also allowed the clarification of various integrals and series, although this tends to be difficult a priori.

Finally they make it possible to solve integral equations of the form 

: <math>f(x)=\int_0^1\frac{g(t)-g(x)}{t-x}\rho(t)\,dt</math>

where ''g'' is the unknown function, and lead to theorems of convergence towards the [[Chebyshev]] and [[Dirac measure]]s.

==The broad outlines of the theory==

Let ρ be a measure of positive [[density]] on an interval I and admitting moments of any order. From this, a family {''P<sub>n</sub>''} of [[orthogonal polynomials]] for the [[inner product]] induced by ρ can be created.  

Let {''Q<sub>n</sub>''} be the sequence of the secondary polynomials associated with the family ''P''.  Under certain conditions there is a measure for which the family ''Q'' is orthogonal. This measure, which can be clarified from ρ, is called a secondary measure associated initial measure ρ.

When ρ is a [[probability density function]], a sufficient condition that allows μ to be a secondary measure associated with ρ while admitting moments of any order is that its [[Stieltjes]] Transformation is given by an equality of the type

: <math>S_{\mu}(z)=a\left(z-c_1-\frac{1}{S_{\rho}(z)}\right),</math>

where ''a'' is an arbitrary constant and ''c''<sub>1</sub> indicates the moment of order 1 of ρ.

For ''a'' = 1, '''the''' measure known as secondary can be obtained.  For ''n'' ≥ 1 the [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] of the polynomial ''P<sub>n</sub>'' for ρ coincides exactly with the norm of the secondary polynomial associated ''Q<sub>n</sub>'' when using the measure μ.

In this paramount case, and if the space generated by the orthogonal polynomials is [[dense set|dense]] in ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''I'', '''R''', ρ), the [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]] ''T''<sub>ρ</sub> defined by 

:<math>f(x) \mapsto \int_I \frac{f(t)-f(x)}{t-x}\rho (t)dt</math> 

creating the secondary polynomials can be furthered to a [[linear map]] connecting space ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''I'', '''R''', ρ) to ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''I'', '''R''', μ) and becomes isometric if limited to the [[hyperplane]] ''H''<sub>ρ</sub> of the [[orthogonal functions]] with ''P''<sub>0</sub> = 1.

For unspecified functions [[square integrable]] for ρ a more general formula of [[covariance]] may be obtained:

: <math> \langle f/g \rangle_\rho - \langle f/1 \rangle_\rho\times \langle g/1\rangle_\rho = \langle T_\rho(f)/T_\rho (g) \rangle_\mu.</math>

The theory continues by introducing the concept of reducible measure, meaning that the quotient ρ/μ is element of ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''I'', '''R''', μ). The following results are then established:

*The reducer φ of ρ is an antecedent of ρ/μ for the operator ''T''<sub>ρ</sub>. (In fact the only antecedent which belongs to ''H''<sub>ρ</sub>).

*For any function square integrable for ρ, there is an equality known as the reducing formula: 

:<math> \langle f/\varphi \rangle_\rho = \langle T_\rho (f)/1 \rangle_\rho</math>.

*The operator 
:<math>f\mapsto \varphi\times f -T_\rho (f)</math> 
:defined on the polynomials is prolonged in an [[isometry]] ''S''<sub>ρ</sub> linking the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of the space of these polynomials in ''L''<sup>2</sup>(''I'', '''R''', ρ<sup>2</sup>μ<sup>−1</sup>)  to the [[hyperplane]] ''H''<sub>ρ</sub> provided with the norm induced by ρ.

*Under certain restrictive conditions the operator ''S''<sub>ρ</sub> acts like the [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] of ''T''<sub>ρ</sub> for the [[inner product]] induced by ρ.

Finally the two operators are also connected, provided the images in question are defined, by the fundamental formula of composition:

: <math>T_\rho\circ S_\rho \left( f\right)=\frac{\rho}{\mu}\times (f).</math>

==Case of the Lebesgue measure and some other examples==
The [[Lebesgue]] measure on the standard interval [0, 1] is obtained by taking the constant density ρ(''x'') = 1.

The associated [[orthogonal polynomials]] are called [[Legendre polynomials#Shifted_Legendre_polynomials|(shifted) Legendre polynomials]] and can be defined as
<math display="block">
  P_n(x)=\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\left(x^n(1-x)^n\right).
</math> 
The [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] of these ''P<sub>n</sub>'' is then
<math display="block">
  \frac{n!}{\sqrt{2n+1}}
</math> 
and the recurrence relation in three terms can be written
<math display="block">
  2(2n+1)xP_n(x)=-P_{n+1}(x)+(2n+1)P_n(x)-n^2P_{n-1}(x).
</math>

The reducer of this measure of Lebesgue is given by 

:<math>\varphi(x)=2\ln\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right).</math>

The associated secondary measure is then clarified as 

:<math>\mu(x)=\frac{1}{\ln^2\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)+\pi^2}</math>.

If we normalize the polynomials of Legendre, the coefficients of [[Fourier analysis|Fourier]] of the reducer φ related to this orthonormal system are null for an even index and are given by 

:<math>C_n(\varphi)=-\frac{4\sqrt{2n+1}}{n(n+1)}</math> 

for an odd index ''n''.

The [[Laguerre polynomials]] are linked to the density ρ(''x'') = ''e<sup>−x</sup>'' on the interval ''I'' = [0, ∞). They are clarified by

: <math>L_n(x)=\frac{e^x}{n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^ne^{-x})=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(-1)^k\frac{x^k}{k!}</math>

and are normalized.

The reducer associated is defined by

: <math>\varphi(x)=2\left (\ln(x)-\int_0^{\infty}e^{-t}\ln|x-t|dt\right ).</math>

The  coefficients of Fourier of the reducer φ related to the Laguerre polynomials are given by  

: <math>C_n(\varphi)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\binom{n-1}{k}}.</math>

This coefficient ''C<sub>n</sub>''(φ) is no other than the opposite of the sum of the elements of the line of index ''n'' in the table of the harmonic triangular numbers of [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Leibniz]]. 

The [[Hermite]] polynomials are linked to the [[Gaussian density]]

: <math>\rho(x)=\frac{e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}</math> 

on ''I'' = '''R'''.

They are clarified by

: <math>H_n(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n!}}e^{\frac{x^2}{2}}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\left(e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}\right)</math>

and are normalized.

The reducer associated is defined by

: <math>\varphi(x)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}te^{-\frac{t^2}{2}}\ln|x-t|\,dt.</math>

The coefficients of [[Fourier analysis|Fourier]] of the reducer φ related to the system of [[Hermite polynomials]] are null for an even index and are given by

: <math>C_n(\varphi)=(-1)^{\frac{n+1}{2}}\frac{\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)!}{\sqrt{n!}}</math>

for an odd index ''n''.

The [[Chebyshev]] measure of the second form.  This is defined by the density 

:<math>\rho(x)=\frac{8}{\pi}\sqrt{x(1-x)}</math> 

on the interval [0, 1].

It is the only one which coincides with its secondary measure normalised on this standard interval. Under certain conditions it occurs as the limit of the sequence of normalized secondary measures of a given density.

===Examples of non-reducible measures===

Jacobi measure on (0, 1) of density 

:<math>\rho(x)=\frac{2}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{x}}.</math> 

Chebyshev measure on (−1,&nbsp;1) of the first form of density 

:<math>\rho(x)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-x^2}}.</math>

==Sequence of secondary measures==
The secondary measure μ associated with a [[probability density function]] ρ has its moment of order 0 given by the formula 

:<math>d_0 = c_2 -c_1^2, </math> 

where ''c''<sub>1</sub> and ''c''<sub>2</sub> indicating the respective moments of order 1 and 2 of ρ. 

This process can be iterated by 'normalizing' μ while defining ρ<sub>1</sub> = μ/''d''<sub>0</sub> which becomes in its turn a density of probability called naturally the normalised secondary measure associated with ρ.

From ρ<sub>1</sub>, a secondary normalised measure ρ<sub>2</sub> can be created. This can be iterated to obtain ρ<sub>3</sub> from ρ<sub>2</sub> and so on.

Therefore, a sequence of successive secondary measures, created from ρ<sub>0</sub> = ρ, is such that ρ<sub>''n''+1</sub> that is the secondary normalised measure deduced from ρ<sub>''n''</sub>

It is possible to clarify the density ρ<sub>''n''</sub> by using the [[orthogonal polynomials]] ''P<sub>n</sub>'' for ρ, the secondary polynomials ''Q<sub>n</sub>'' and the reducer associated φ. This gives the formula

: <math>\rho_n(x)=\frac{1}{d_0^{n-1}} \frac{\rho(x)}{\left(P_{n-1}(x) \frac{\varphi(x)}{2}-Q_{n-1}(x)\right)^2 + \pi^2\rho^2(x) P_{n-1}^2(x)}.</math>

The coefficient <math>d_0^{n-1}</math> is easily obtained starting from the leading coefficients of the polynomials ''P''<sub>''n''−1</sub> and ''P<sub>n</sub>''. The reducer φ<sub>''n''</sub> associated with ρ<sub>''n''</sub>, as well as the orthogonal polynomials corresponding to ρ<sub>''n''</sub>, can also be clarified.

The evolution of these densities when the index tends towards the infinite can be related to the support of the measure on the standard interval [0, 1]:

Let 
:<math>xP_n (x)=t_nP_{n+1}(x)+s_nP_n(x)+t_{n-1}P_{n-1}(x)</math> 
be the classic recurrence relation in three terms. If  

:<math>\lim_{n \mapsto \infty} t_n=\tfrac{1}{4}, \quad \lim_{n \mapsto \infty} s_n =\tfrac{1}{2},</math> 

then the sequence {ρ<sub>''n''</sub>} converges completely towards the [[Chebyshev]] density of the second form 

:<math>\rho_{tch}(x)=\frac{8}{\pi}\sqrt{x(1-x)}</math>.

These conditions about limits are checked by a very broad class of traditional densities.
A derivation of the sequence of secondary measures and convergence can be found in.<ref name ="Arxiv secondary measure article" />

===Equinormal measures===
One calls two measures thus leading to the same normalised secondary density. It is remarkable that the elements of a given class and having the same moment of order 1 are connected by a homotopy. More precisely, if the density function ρ has its moment of order 1 equal to ''c''<sub>1</sub>, then these densities equinormal with ρ are given by a formula of the type:  

:<math>\rho_{t}(x)=\frac{t\rho(x)}{\left (\tfrac{1}{2}(t-1)(x-c_1)\varphi(x)-t\right )^2+\pi^2\rho^2(x)(t-1)^2(x-c_1)^2},</math> 

''t'' describing an interval containing ]0, 1].

If μ is the secondary measure of ρ, that of ρ<sub>''t''</sub> will be ''t''μ.

The reducer of ρ<sub>''t''</sub> is

:<math>\varphi_t(x)=\frac{2 (x-c_1)-tG(x)}{\left((x-c_1)-t\tfrac{1}{2}G(x) \right)^2+t^2\pi^2\mu^2(x)}</math> 

by noting ''G''(''x'') the reducer of μ.

Orthogonal polynomials for the measure ρ<sub>''t''</sub> are clarified from ''n'' = 1 by the formula

: <math>P_n^t(x)=\frac{tP_n(x)+(1-t)(x-c_1)Q_n(x)}{\sqrt{t}}</math> 

with ''Q<sub>n</sub>'' secondary polynomial associated with ''P<sub>n</sub>''.

It is remarkable also that, within the meaning of distributions, the limit when ''t'' tends towards 0 per higher value of ρ<sub>''t''</sub> is the Dirac measure concentrated at ''c''<sub>1</sub>. 

For example, the equinormal densities with the Chebyshev measure of the second form are defined by: 

:<math>\rho_t(x)=\frac{2t\sqrt{1-x^2}}{\pi\left[t^2+4(1-t)x^2\right]},</math>

with ''t'' describing ]0, 2]. The value ''t'' = 2  gives the Chebyshev measure of the first form.

==Applications==
In the formulas below ''G'' is [[Catalan's constant]], γ is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant|Euler's constant]], β<sub>2''n''</sub> is the [[Bernoulli number]] of order 2''n'', ''H''<sub>2''n''+1</sub> is the [[harmonic number]] of order 2''n''+1 and Ei is the [[Exponential integral]] function.

: <math>\frac{1}{\ln(p)} = \frac{1}{p-1}+\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{(x+p)(\ln^2(x)+\pi^2)} dx \qquad \qquad \forall p > 1</math>
: <math>\gamma = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln(1+\frac{1}{x})}{\ln^2(x)+\pi^2} dx</math>
: <math>\gamma = \frac{1}{2}+\int_0^{\infty} \frac{\overline {(x+1)\cos(\pi x)}}{x+1} dx</math>

The notation <math>x\mapsto \overline {(x+1)\cos(\pi x)}</math> indicating the 2 [[periodic function]] coinciding with <math>x\mapsto (x+1) \cos(\pi x)</math> on (−1, 1).

:<math>\gamma = \frac{1}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{\beta_{2k}}{2k} - \frac{\beta_{2n}}{\zeta(2n)}\int_1^{\infty} \lfloor t \rfloor \cos(2\pi t) t^{-2n-1} dt</math>
:<math>\beta_k = \frac{(-1)^kk!}{\pi} \text{Im} \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^x}{(1+e^x)(x-i\pi)^k} dx \right)</math>
:<math>\int_0^1\ln^{2n}\left(\frac{x}{1-x}\right)\,dx = (-1)^{n+1}(2^{2n}-2)\beta_{2n}\pi^{2n}</math>
:<math>\int_0^1\cdots \int_0^1 \left(\sum_{k=1}^{2n} \frac{\ln(t_k)}{\prod_{i \neq k}(t_k-t_i)}\right)\, dt_1 \cdots dt_{2n}=\tfrac{1}{2}(-1)^{n+1}(2\pi)^{2n}\beta_{2n}</math>
:<math>\int_0^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\alpha x}}{\Gamma(x+1)}dx = e^{e^{-\alpha}}-1+\int_0^{\infty} \frac{1-e^{-x}}{(\ln(x)+\alpha)^2+\pi^2}\frac{dx}{x} \qquad \qquad \forall \alpha \in \mathbf{R}</math>
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{1}{\binom{n-1}{k}}\right)^2=\tfrac{4}{9}\pi^2=\int_0^{\infty}4 \left (\mathrm {Ei} (1,-x)+i\pi \right )^2 e^{-3x} \, dx.</math>
:<math>\frac{23}{15}-\ln(2) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1575}{2(n+1)(2n+1)(4n-3)(4n-1)(4n+1)(4n+5)(4n+7)(4n+9)}</math>
:<math>G= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{4^{k+1}} \left(\frac{1}{(4k+3)^2}+\frac{2}{(4k+2)^2}+\frac{2}{(4k+1)^2}\right)+\frac{\pi}{8}\ln(2)</math>
:<math>G= \frac{\pi}{8}\ln(2)+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{H_{2n+1}}{2n+1}.</math>

If the measure ρ is reducible and let φ be the associated reducer, one has the equality

: <math>\int_I\varphi^2(x)\rho(x) \, dx = \frac{4\pi^2}{3}\int_I\rho^3(x) \, dx.</math>

If the measure ρ is reducible with μ the associated reducer, then if ''f'' is [[square integrable]] for μ, and if ''g'' is square integrable for ρ and is orthogonal with ''P''<sub>0</sub> = 1, the following equivalence holds:

:<math>f(x)=\int_I\frac{g(t)-g(x)}{t-x}\rho(t)dt \Leftrightarrow g(x)=(x-c_1)f(x)-T_{\mu}(f(x))=\frac{\varphi(x)\mu(x)}{\rho(x)}f(x)-T_{\rho} \left(\frac{\mu(x)}{\rho(x)}f(x)\right)</math>

''c''<sub>1</sub> indicates the moment of order 1 of ρ and ''T''<sub>ρ</sub> the operator

:<math>g(x)\mapsto \int_I\frac{g(t)-g(x)}{t-x}\rho(t)\,dt.</math>
In addition, the sequence of secondary measures has applications in Quantum Mechanics, where it gives rise to the ''sequence of residual spectral densities'' for specialized Pauli-Fierz [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonians]]. This also provides a physical interpretation for the sequence of secondary measures. <ref name ="Arxiv secondary measure article" />
